items.title: First of its kind: A World Series preview
items.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
items.content:
The matchup of the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays guarantees a Fall Classic first. Over the next week or so, baseball will deliver unto one of these franchises and fanbases its first World Series celebration.

“First” is one of the best words you can encounter in sports, and “place in the standings” might be its least intriguing application. Like a third-base coach touching his nose or tapping his belt, “first” is an indicator signal for a fun fact about to be delivered.

Entry level versions follow the “first … since …” format. The thing has been done before, but perhaps the time elapsed or the last team/player to accomplish it makes it interesting. A pitcher throwing a compete game would be the first complete game since Yoshinobu Yamamoto in 2025. Yeah, not that interesting. A champion clinching in its home ballpark would be the first since 2022 and only the second since 2013. OK, weird.

Relentlessly deployed Brewers fireman Aaron Ashby might have a shot at a fun one, if the series cooperates: First pitcher to pitch in seven games of a World Series since Brandon Morrow in 2017, or first pitcher to  in seven games of a World Series since Darold Knowles in 1974. That would be something!

But for this preview, I wanted to aim higher, to true beacons of novelty, of revelation, of “I Was There” momentous occasions.

Here are nine firsts that have never happened in the World Series, ranked by likelihood they happen in Brewers-Rays, starting with the most likely.

Some firsts tell us about the conditions of the game. The challenge system is making its World Series debut after a positive and pretty seamless introduction to major-league gameplay.

The top of the first inning of Game 1 will feature William Contreras behind the dish for the Brewers — the most prolific head-tapper of both the regular season (by a healthy margin) and the postseason. There’s a good chance this seal is broken in expedient fashion.

From there, the question becomes how adrenaline and stakes and heightened strategic instructions play on the biggest stage. Already, we’ve seen a significant postseason shift toward saving challenges for catchers. In the regular season, catchers around MLB challenged 5,559 calls to hitters’ 4,765, a 1.17 catcher/batter ratio. In the postseason, that ratio is 1.55.

And with these two teams, the change has looked even more extreme. Brewers have challenged 20 calls, while their batters have challenged 7. And the Rays catchers have challenged 12 calls, while all their hitters have made like Yandy Diaz and refrained from tapping even once (an infinite ratio, if you’re doing the math).

Any close call in a big spot will now have an extra layer of drama: To challenge, or not to challenge?

Some firsts tell us about freakish human achievement. Aroldis Chapman threw the fastest World Series pitch on record (pitch tracking dates to 2008), back in 2016. It was a 103.2 mph fastball on 0-2 that Coco Crisp actually made contact with, grounding out to second base.

Brewers starter and presumptive NL Cy Young Jacob Misiorowski has thrown 100 pitches faster than that one this season, including 28 that broke the 104 mph threshold. This is an excitable young man, in a good way.

His way of saying “Welcome to the NLDS” was chucking 104.8 mph on the first pitch.

He actually broke 104 mph in Game 1 of both the NLDS and the NLCS. The Brewers sweep of the Dodgers means he will be on 11 days rest when he takes the mound for Game 1. Of the World Series. He’s going to throw the ball real fast.

First game to end in 13, 15, 16, or 17 innings

Other firsts tell us about the possibility a die could be mistakenly manufactured with seven dots on one side.

Two different World Series marathons involving the Dodgers have stretched to 18 innings in recent memory, but no games have concluded in several relatively normal-sounding spans before that. Frankly, I would be pro extra-inning scrambling without extreme sleep deprivation. Rooting for this. Let’s see Chad Patrick or Steven Matz or some other very regular pitching contributors from the regular season summoned into high-pressure action, why not?

With the zombie runner excised from postseason competition, more aggressive pitcher usage, and a lower scoring environment ruling the day, a long (but not that long) extra-innings game is probably in the cards for the near future. But we’ve already dropped from “near certainty” to a statistical improbability.

Yoshinobu Yamamoto is not walking through that door. Last season’s complete game was an adrenaline shot straight to the heart for starting pitching junkies, providing the headline for a series that included a lot of good starter performances. The Dodgers and Blue Jays combined for seven starts of six frames or more.

The Brewers’ innings leader this October is the aforementioned Aaron Ashby, a reliever. Manager Pat Murphy has not been inclined to push his uniformly young starters — Misiorowski, Logan Henderson, Robert Gasser — and doesn’t seem likely to alter that stance with veteran Dustin May, the fourth starter. If a Milwaukee arm sees the seventh, it’s probably because he’s doing something historic (more on that later).

The Rays, on the other hand, are rolling a pretty traditional starting rotation and trusting their guys. I’ve lost track of whether that’s a zig or a zag from the club that popularized the opener (wait for it …) eight years ago. Drew Rasmussen is averaging seven innings a start this month. His 21 innings pitched are 4 1/3 innings clear of second place, his teammate Freddy Peralta. But Peralta, an icon of the five-and-dive modern approach, being the second-most-likely candidate is also a recession indicator for starters working deep.

Probably, , at least one starter will have a good night and keep this rather unappealing first at bay. But the bullpen phone is always right there, waiting to ring.

First walk-off walk (or walk-off hit by pitch)

No World Series game has ever ended with a bases-loaded walk or a plunking, which I found a little surprising.

There have been 63 walk-off endings in Fall Classic games. There have been 23 plate appearances across 15 games meeting the conditions to produce a walk-off walk — home team with the bases loaded, ninth inning or later, tie game. In any given 23 plate appearances, even in special conditions, you’d expect to see a walk or a hit by pitch.

The MLB walk rate with the bases loaded was 7.3% in 2026, below the overall 8.9% walk rate, as you would hope, but not by a lot. That gap has been consistent in recent years. Only include high-leverage spots within that sample … like a tie game in the ninth or later would be … and the walk rate ticks down even further to 6.7%. I looked at the last five years for a bigger sample: Combining walk rate and hit-by-pitch rate in high-leverage, bases loaded situations and you’re looking at a 9.8% free pass rate.

It speaks to something about the extreme pressure of that moment, perhaps on both sides of the equation, that we have count information on 21 of the 23 World Series at-bats in this scenario, and none of them have even reached three balls. No one on the mound wants to be the pitching equivalent of Bill Buckner, and everyone in the batter’s box wants to be the latest version of Luis Gonzalez or Freddie Freeman.

This requires a special brew of circumstances to come to fruition: just seven games since 2000 have played out this way. But if it comes up, Milwaukee been steadfast in taking walks this postseason, and in working the count to register three true outcomes across the board. Jake Bauers, he of the multiple 12-pitch at-bats, is running a 20.6% walk rate in the playoffs, and Brice Turang isn’t far behind.

Where a walk will do, a walk-off into history is in play.

First 20-strikeout game (by a team)

Dodgers pitchers struck out 19 Red Sox batters in Game 3 of the 2018 World Series … but that was in 18 innings. The high-water mark in a nine-inning game remain’s Bob Gibson’s 17-K masterpiece in 1968.

But combination whiff-fests are inching closer. The Dodgers struck out 16 in 2020, the Blue Jays struck out 15 last year. The Brewers struck out 20 White Sox batters on Opening Day this year, in a nine-inning game, and also struck out 20 A’s in a 12-inning game in June.

Less than two weeks ago, the Guardians logged 21 strikeouts against the White Sox in ALDS Game 5.

(This first would have ranked higher if the White Sox were involved, clearly.)

First World Series with all games decided by one run

If I’m being honest, this postseason has been relatively short on riveting series and moments. Maybe the best series was the Brewers’ white-knuckle game of chicken with the Padres. Three of those games were one-run affairs, while the fourth and final game was a two-run Brewers win.

The Rays took two of their three games against the Yankees by one run, and the Brewers' dethroning of the Dodgers had its thrills, but both teams have spent much of the month feeling in control. Maybe — here’s hoping — that produces a less controlled environment this week.

It’s not totally implausible. A few Fall Classics have come close. In 1972, six of the seven games were decided by the narrowest of margins as the A’s prevailed over the Reds. And in shorter series, five of six were one-run battles when Atlanta beat Cleveland in 1995. Four of five has happened twice (1915, 1974), while three of four happened once, in 1950.

First walk-off bunt without an error involved

There has been a walk-off bunt, two actually. The most recent was in 1969, when a Mets sacrifice bunt turned into a throwing error and a run and a win. An earlier similar instance came in 1914.

This first is about the bunt winning the game on its own merits. (For the record, there has also not been a late-inning go-ahead bunt of any sort other than the previously mentioned, error-empowered two.)

Bunts are a little bit back in vogue, because athleticism is fun, speed is fun, and it’s hard to score. Look under every rock, right? The Rays and Brewers look under every rock. These two teams led MLB in bunt hits in 2026, with the Rays first at 49 and the Brewers second at 32.

It doesn’t have to be a bunt single necessarily. A wicked fielder’s choice gone awry could work. But even for teams with some small ball tendencies, this doesn’t happen very often. This is a claustrophobic tale of agile underdog excellence, like a gnat escaping a tiny, windowless room by zipping around a man with a flyswatter, dizzying him to the point he falls and knocks himself out while opening the door handle.

His stature has leveled up significantly since that moment (Turang was the fifth-best position player in baseball this year, full stop, by FanGraphs WAR), so I don’t think he’d be  to bunt in that situation. But is there a part of him that would be interested in testing Caminero, the Rays third baseman whose defense graded out ahead of only other six corner infielders this year?

This season, the defense-first Rays shortstop Walls bunted in the tying run in what has to be considered an unusual bunting situation — runners on second and third, no one out, 10th inning — against the Yankees in April.

Add in Simpson’s “any bunt could just be a hit” speed, Mullins’ proclivity for surprise bunts and Hamilton’s bench bat positioning for the Brewers, and the possibility exists. More than in any other recent series, that’s for sure.

First 20-strikeout game (by a pitcher)

Self-explanatory, really. The 20-strikeout game (in nine innings) is less common than a perfect game, more exquisite than a four-homer night. Only four pitchers have done it (Roger Clemens did it twice). Gibson’s 17-strikeout World Series shutout in 1968 is the all-time record in a postseason game. That’s one of only seven playoff games where a pitcher got to 15.

It’s not happening. But if it did … would Jacob Misiorowski not be the candidate? He just finished off a season with a 37.9 K%, the second-best rate by a qualified starter in a full season, behind Gerrit Cole’s 2019. He doesn’t really give up runs. He is amply rested, 24 years old and hyped.

Maybe there’s no such thing as a candidate for this before he’s on the mound, throwing the game of his life, of all our lives. Maybe there’s a first time for everything. ⚾️

items.title: How we help make sure your vote counts
items.author: SRS0=sMxO=IL=bh1234.vbnewsletters.votebeat.org=bounces+misc=muneer.top@eforward.registrar-servers.com
items.content:
Election rules vary state to state. Votebeat helps voters make sense of them.  ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌

Voting and elections have a lot of specific rules and regulations that — because U.S. elections are very decentralized — can change based on where you live.

Rules that vary across the country include: the dates and times early voting may be available, whether no-excuse absentee voting is an option, and requirements for voter ID on Election Day.

Elections are locally run and so various state laws determine a lot about how and when voters are able to vote. That’s why Votebeat is primarily local. We have five reporters embedded in key states across the country: Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Texas, and Wisconsin.

My colleagues are specialized in knowing exactly how elections are run where they live — and they are the first to tell you if any of these rules have changed or are creating hurdles for voters at the polls.

items.title: Leadership Dispatch: Co-lead strategically
items.author: bounces+68ummn4ex9s8h5qmdlgaohppxkqm7h9hgzo3@ckespa.joshdoody.com
items.content:
This week's Leadership Dispatch is about co-leadership. Managing your relationship with co-leaders may be more nuanced than leading a group. Think strategically about your relationship with your co-leaders, and how you portray the leadership team to the team you are leading.

Before you begin co-leading, you should decide whether there is a hierarchy or whether all leaders are co-equal. If you are the ultimate leader and they are leaders who are also part of your team, then lead your co-leaders as you would other team members.

But if you are co-equal, meaning that you and your co-leaders will generally have equal say, then the approach changes slightly. You’ll need to operate in a more collaborative way and defer more frequently than you would if you were the only leader.

You will find that you don’t have a strong opinion on many decisions. On those decisions, you should just defer to your co-leaders.

Occasionally, you have a strong opinion on a decision, and that is the time to cash in on the social capital you’ve accumulated by being deferential most of the time. If you almost always defer to your co-leaders, then when you suddenly have a strong opinion and do not immediately defer, that will carry a lot of weight.

You should ultimately portray your leadership team as a single unit so that your team perceives you and your co-leaders to be in lockstep, even if you are not.

items.title: Rayfabe
items.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
items.content:
Here’s an incomplete list of things that happened after Junior Caminero, the 23-year-old Rays slugger, hit what appeared to be a back-breaking two-run homer off the foul pole in the seventh inning of ALCS Game 6:

Short of and to the crowd side of first base, Caminero stopped, leaned back, closed his eyes and pounded his chest with both fists — a move reminiscent of Disney movie Tarzan.

He cupped his hand to his ear rounding second, imploring the Tropicana Field crowd to keep roaring.

In the top of the eighth, Guardians star Jose Ramirez popped out weakly to center field, and then sat defeated on the dugout bench, straining to envision a different outcome on the ceiling, in the depths of his head.

But then … Chase DeLauter beat out a grounder to first. Nathaniel Lowe singled. The Rays brought in Ian Seymour to pitch. He promptly walked Travis Bazzana and and Patrick Bailey, then plunked Angel Martinez, forcing in two runs. The Caminero homer was essentially erased.

Another pitching change got the Rays out of the jam, still up two.

Shortly thereafter, Diaz, baseball’s reigning god of protein, consumed a tomahawk steak like an ice cream cone during the clubhouse celebration.

The Rays are going to the World Series, and they made a meal out of it.

What little I know about professional wrestling, I have absorbed accidentally. But the final two frames of the ALCS were unmistakable. A haymaking blow from a main character, full minutes of time spent celebrating and heralding that split-second achievement, a rapid series of barely believable events rendering that triumph essentially moot, a new haymaker thrown, a coronation, a promo cut on the microphone.

Maybe it’s the sheer size of Caminero and Diaz. Maybe it’s the color pop of the Devil Rays alternate uniforms Tampa has adopted for this run. Maybe it’s the freezer-aisle-at-Costco lighting of Tropicana Field. This baseball game became pro wrestling. And that felt good, actually, felt right.

Tampa Bay has fielded successful teams many, many times without necessarily filling the rafters at the poorly placed dome in St. Petersburg, and often without inspiring more admiration than what you’d offer for a particularly onerous mathematical advancement. The Rays’ deep postseason runs, though, have come with extra park-adjusted oomph that animates their excellence — a sort of lie that amplifies the truth. What I’ve come to understand as .

In wrestling, kayfabe is the art of fully buying into the fiction for an audience that knows the production is staged. The baseball isn’t staged, but there’s value in extracting the unspoken tension trapped in scorecards and clenched jaw muscles and firing it out of a T-shirt cannon into plain sight, onto the field.

It’s charisma and catharsis layered on top of the careful execution.

Like Arozarena before him, Caminero is bringing the Rayfabe. Play-by-play announcer Brian Anderson said this during the post-homer rancor, but you might have missed it: That was the first homer anyone has ever hit off Cade Smith’s splitter in major-league action, regular or postseason, the lone long ball out of 884 pitches.

Cartoon adaptations are possible throughout the clubhouse — Chandler Simpson’s speed; Victor Mesa Jr.’s rocket arm and little-brother-made-good story; the pitching staff of untouchable everyman clones; Diaz’s stoic, cuddly bodybuilder persona — that build on the productive, precise skills underneath. With two 40-homer seasons under his belt at, again, the age of 23, Caminero is the face. He’s a craftsman and a hype man.

Under new ownership and plotting a move, at long last, to a more conveniently located ballpark, a moment like this is bigger for the Rays than it would be for most other clubs. A decade or more of front office mastery wins a lot of games, but doesn’t necessarily inspire the legions. I’d like to think this sort of display, packed into just a few weeks, could move that latter needle.

It was fascinating that Arozarena, an impending free agent who has been with the Seattle Mariners, and Tyler Glasnow, a Rays avatar turned Dodgers starter, were in the stands to support the franchise. Glasnow, who departed after 2023, was teammates with Caminero for all of seven games. Arozarena was there a half-season longer, but still had only marginal time with what’s now the core of this group.

Despite the constant churn, the packed bags and the often half-full dome, there’s a longer-term tale in Tampa. They help players find the best versions of themselves, help them identify and unleash something inside. Something about that connection clearly sticks for the guys who have been there and left. You wonder if someday, with more money or more support or more of whatever it will take to achieve either of those things, it might manifest itself in ways that go beyond just  Rays.

I don’t know what ending I’d script for the franchise’s Tropicana Field era.

In the dome, you can sense that the conditions are weird and subpar, but also special. Every iota of attention is earned and paid off. The show has to be fully mustered from the talents of the performers. There’s an underdog quality, even when they are clearly the best team in the American League.

Another thing I’ve picked up about wrestling: The crowd’s favorite doesn’t always win, but a strong character development can alter the future.

The part where I ask for your support

This is a project by and for the passionate. It’s undertaken on mornings, nights and weekends. On trains and planes and holidays. Around the responsibilities of a full-time job.

I recognize the building subscription creep, the proliferation of good writers operating independently and charging independently in an unforgiving industry. I don’t expect The Bandwagon to be your only destination for baseball writing, but I hope it makes your emotional investment more enriching.

items.title: Sweater: Here for It, #
items.author: SRS0=G82P=II=m.ghost.io=bounce+3cffae.7bdc18-misc=muneer.top@eforward.registrar-servers.com
items.content:
Hi! It's R. Eric Thomas. From the internet?Hi!

Oh, everyone in the Northeast went into their cedar chest and pulled out their lil Say Something Sweater this weekend I see!

Yes, folks felt a little chill in the air and they said, "lemme go on and hit the people with a Personality Wool right quick."

Baby, you better go on with your bad self and your Deliciously Chunky Knit or Cozy Cashmere Cowl Neck.

Yes, perhaps it does have the slightest lingering aroma of the dryer sheets you use instead of mothballs to keep your clothes fresh over the winter and yes, it did get a little warm in the sweater in the middle of the day, and yes, tromping all over hither and thither, apple-picking or errand-running or selecting fixtures for your Nancy Meyers-esque kitchen or whatever it is you get up to makes it harder for you to just sit and in this, your Debut Sweater of the Season. But nevertheless, it had to be done. You know she's going to bring it to you every fall!

If you're reading this in someplace that's warm, like Los Angeles or Texas or on top of the Burj Khalifa, you are probably not on board with what I'm talking about but I believe that, spiritually, we are aligned. There comes a time in every year when you're like, I've decided to participate in fall. Alert the proper authorities.

I might wear cranberry. I might wear canary. I might wear marigold. I might wear olive. You have to be prepared to hold all of those possibilities. I am not in control. The Sweater has an energy all its own.

It may not have been the first sweater you wore this year. In fact, it probably wasn't. The Say Something Sweater is the mayor of Knitsburgh. It spends the summer ruling over that little vacuum-sealed bag you keep it in with fairness but firmness. I don't really understand what Soft Power means, but I presume it's about the interior hierarchy of your sweaters and assorted bulky transitional season garments and et cetera.

I don't really know why I'm writing so much about Sweaters, to be honest. It's been so long since I wrote this newsletter and now I'm like "hello, yes, I'd like to speak with you about something that probably only exists in my mind."

I just love Sweaters so much. And I do feel there's a difference between the Say Something Sweater and the Utility Knits, which I define as a sweater--usually a neutral color--that you just don't think about. It's functional. It's warm. It's for work or for church or for yard work and it's fine but it doesn't insist upon itself.

The Say Something Sweater is for when you're fully feeling the fantasy. It might be a bolder color or a more complicated pattern. I feel like Aran sweaters are often Say Something Sweaters, the most famous examples being Billy Crystal's in

And Chris Evans's in .

Fair Isle Sweaters are often also Say Something Sweaters but they have yet to have a truly groundbreaking cinematic moment as far as I'm concerned.

I feel like it's like this: sometimes you're wearing the costume of your life and sometimes you're just dressing. (And I want to add an important caveat: I do not know what I'm talking about I do think I'm correct.)

There are Say Something Sweaters for Fall and Say Something Sweaters for Winter and they are the same.

Holiday sweaters are a whole different category and I do not, at present, have the capacity to get into it. I appreciate your patience.

Anyway, thanks for taking my call. I'll be back next week. I'll probably be talking about something other than Sweaters. But honestly, you never know with me.

I do not know what I'm talking about I do think I'm correct,Eric

items.title: Voters face flurry of ballot measures that could transform elections across the country
items.author: SRS0=la73=IH=bh1234.vbnewsletters.votebeat.org=bounces+misc=muneer.top@eforward.registrar-servers.com
items.content: In another setback for Trump’s efforts to inject more federal control into elections, a federal judge last week to check state voter rolls against federal immigration databases. Judge Sparkle Sooknanan’s found the U.S. Department of Justice’s efforts to collect voter rolls from states and use them to check for noncitizens illegally casting ballots is illegal. Most states refused to comply, often citing privacy laws, though some states agreed to give the Trump administration unredacted voter rolls.  Courts have so far dismissed 26 Justice Department lawsuits seeking to force  states to comply. The ruling constricts the Trump administration from using its Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, program, a federal tool the administration was using to verify voter citizenship once it obtained the voter rolls. This week, Votebeat spoke to Jonathan Diaz, director of voting advocacy and partnerships at the Campaign Legal Center, about the implications.

items.title: The Brewers had the means to end the Dodgers
items.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
items.content:
“They may have a bunch of Hall of Famers, but we’ve got a bunch of gamers.” - Pat Murphy, Brewers manager

They’ve gotten good at it.

Since 2018, when Christian Yelich arrived and kickstarted the current era of Brewers baseball into motion, they have the fourth-most wins in baseball. Since 2023, when top executive David Stearns stepped down and handed the reins to Matt Arnold, they’re second behind the Dodgers. Since 2024, when Craig Counsell left and Pat Murphy stepped into the manager’s role, they’re first.

In the meantime, they ran into failure, and they learned and got better and ran into failure again. They tried things that worked, hit limits — three times dressed in Dodger blue — and pushed and found more things that worked and pushed until they discovered exactly where they stopped working.

The whole process was not easy, was better and more productive for not being easy. You’ll see Brewers players talk about it, about Murphy’s standards and the expectations that can grate on them over the longest, most rigorous season in sports.

“You have to be a certain kind of player to play for Murph and to play here,” Yelich told reporters in August, after Murphy pulled rookie shortstop Cooper Pratt from a game for a lack of hustle. “You couldn’t coach that way throughout the league. You really couldn’t.”

You can see it in Murphy’s strategic needling of his own team, cutting violently away at anything that might dull their focus. And you can see it in his gentle praise, his doting in moments of doubt.

“All I know is that on Aug. 12, we have the best record in baseball,” Murphy said right after the Brewers got swept by the Padres, right before they went to Dodger Stadium and took a confidence-building three of four. “And if you've got the best record in baseball, you're still going to go through times like this when things aren't very good, and everything seems to go against you. But it's in your head that things are going against you.”

They practiced, got called out when they fell short, and practiced, and got praised when they hit their marks.

Last year, it led to 97 wins in the regular season, the most in baseball, but they got trounced four times in a row against the Dodgers. This year, the Brewers won 103 times in the regular season, the most in baseball, again. Faced with the Dodgers, again, they won four times in a row, and they’re going to the World Series.

“The end justifies the means. But what if there never is an end? All we have is means.” - Ursula K. Le Guin, 

If a genie or a god or a world-altering dream granted median baseball fans three wishes this spring, I think the most common ask would have been for their team to win the World Series, and the next most common would have been for the Dodgers  to win the World Series. A particularly enraged few might have asked for the Dodgers’ demise ahead of all else. And an even smaller, more conspiracy-brained sect would have sought the opposite: A third straight championship for the Dodgers, with the conviction it would create more conducive conditions for the introduction of a salary cap and a lasting shift in fortunes for their team.

Watching a physically compromised Shohei Ohtani lunge and flail through this postseason, watching him do everything but break down in the batter’s box, I was struck by the foolishness of those wishes, of the human impulse to overestimate our understanding of what we want.

The Dodgers being out is not the good part, not really. To seek a good outcome above all else is to disregard how you get there.

Baseball is too hard and too interesting to be squished into the tiny form of a pawn on a chessboard. It isn’t a game of design and construction so much as sculpture. The season sands teams down to an essence that can only be partly planned. It grinds away at players who absorb the losses, then struggle to shape what’s left into something productive.

The Brewers practiced and practiced. Through grit and grind and greatness, they sharpened themselves into a winning instrument that will be judged by the intrinsic value experienced on the field and on the screen, not for the money spent in creating it.

It must be said that the Dodgers did a version of the same, repeatedly molding and wielding the game’s heaviest blunt force object to generationally great effect. Last season, the Dodgers overwhelmed the Brewers, but needed every ounce of might to get past the Blue Jays. Only in that struggle did we achieve our fullest appreciation of what they could do, of their means. The end came at the last possible moment, and still far too soon.

When the Brewers came calling for this year’s rematch, the weakened Dodgers were the ones overwhelmed. The Brewers won this round decisively, but it didn’t feel like a grand conclusion. It felt like a simple demonstration of physics, like a wasted wish.

“There is no avoiding the fight, because stupid will blame the sheep for inciting the wolves.” - Spencer Hall, 

Major League Baseball, and the team owners whose interests it represents, has spent the year trying to convince the viewing public that baseball is like Rock, Paper, Scissors. The brute force of high payrolls and big markets will always crush the scissors of leaner operations, and no one in their billionaire’s club has the paper to overcome the rocks.

Scissors slicing up rock on the sport’s biggest stage won’t change a damn thing about what they want or what they do next. They’re going to chase the financial boon of self-imposed spending limits, possibly at the expense of playing the games, and they’re going to go on saying that the fans want them to do it. They were going to do and say that all along, whether anyone wanted it or not.

That they have successfully misled so many interested onlookers is the saddest, most infuriating part, and that it's so immaterial to their only interest (money) makes it worse. The sport earns its interest so relentlessly that they can self-sabotage to grow their margins.

There are baseball fans spending their precious emotional energy on rooting to watch less of Ohtani in his prime, on rooting for or against a flattened caricature, on trying to channel their interest through a convoluted string on a deranged cork board that never pointed to anything except more guaranteed riches for the richest people involved. Worse, there are fans convinced they didn’t want to watch at all who will be stunned — “stun” is the Brewers-inspired euphemistic verb of the moment for the Brewers, briefly supplanting “loom” as it relates to the lockout — that the best team in baseball just dispatched the Dodgers.

The pennant-winning Brewers are only stunning if you have missed the whole point, if you have been convinced to follow a boring, pointless shadow puppet routine staged 10 stories above the action. They are not a stand-in for small markets or a team-building philosophy or a piece in a billion-dollar game.

They are just a great team that practices what remains the oldest and best advice available in baseball: Keep your eye on the ball. ⚾️

The part where I ask for your support

This is a project by and for the passionate. It’s undertaken on mornings, nights and weekends. On trains and planes and holidays. Around the responsibilities of a full-time job.

I recognize the building subscription creep, the proliferation of good writers operating independently and charging independently in an unforgiving industry. I don’t expect The Bandwagon to be your only destination for baseball writing, but I hope it makes your emotional investment more enriching.

items.title: New from Chicago: An urgent call to turn from broken economics
items.author: 555618737.1998257.813949133233@e2ma.net
items.content:
Acclaimed economist James K. Galbraith sounds an urgent alarm: how conventional economic ideas and policies are unequipped to account for the most daunting challenges of our geopolitical moment.

Amid a mounting sense of American decline, Americans live with a new kind of dissonance: economists announcing that everything is fundamentally fine. Where growth is steady, unemployment is low, prices are (somewhat) stable, and stocks are high—what’s there to worry about? 

shows that this dissonance reflects a failure to evolve. James K. Galbraith’s incisive history of economic policy in this century is grounded in the fundamental problem that today’s experts are still deploying tools from all yesterday’s wars: obsolete economic ideas, measures, and doctrines focused on market functioning and crude economic indicators like output and prices. These methods, many of them honed a century ago against a vastly different social landscape, offer little hope in the face of today’s more existential threats. 

Such conventional policies, Galbraith argues, are increasingly ill-equipped to counter the daunting challenges of our moment—from inflation to trade sanctions, industrial cold wars, and climate change—and, left unacknowledged, are accelerating the end of the US economy as we know it. Shortcomings include the weak responses to the inflation of 2021–2022; the sanctions war against Russia; the rise of China; the weak and ineffective attempt at industrial revival; and the impending demographic crisis. All have roots in a flawed body of outdated economic thought that has been sustained for ideological rather than practical reasons. They now promise to hinder the United States in the emerging multipolar world. 

As Galbraith makes plain, for all the virtues of the market system, governments and their policies make markets possible. The ideas behind the policies—for better or worse—will determine the fate of the US economy—and new and better ideas are urgently needed. The alternative—sticking with economic ideas and policies we know and currently use—brings the power to destroy us all.
